summary.text: Ancient Greece was a civilization of culturally and linguistically related city-states, centered on the northeastern Mediterranean, lasting from the Greek Dark Ages to the end of classical antiquity.
Its city-states, called poleis, began to form in the 8th century BC, and the absence of powerful states plus mountains between settlements encouraged small independent cities.
Classical Greek culture, especially philosophy, strongly influenced Rome, which is why Classical Greece is generally considered the cradle of Western civilization.

items.prompt: Greek settlements sat in valleys cut off from each other by mountains, and no strong state remained after Mycenaean power collapsed. What political pattern would you expect?

options.label: One large kingdom ruling from a single capital
Many small self-governing city-states
A set of cities all ruled by one distant emperor
Scattered villages with no shared political life

items.explain: The lack of powerful states and the mountainous terrain that separated settlements encouraged small independent city-states.

items.prompt: Historians know far more about Athens than about most other Greek cities. What is the main reason?

Athens was the only Greek city with a written language

Athens was the largest Greek city in every period

items.explain: The writers who followed Herodotus were mostly Athenian or pro-Athenian, so far more is known about Athens.

items.prompt: A student treats Herodotus as perfectly reliable because he is called the father of history. What is the fair response?

options.label: His title proves each of his claims was checked and confirmed
He wrote the oldest record of any kind in the ancient world
His work named the field, yet its accuracy is still debated
He wrote only about events of his own lifetime, so no doubt remains

items.explain: Herodotus' Histories gave the field its name, but the accuracy of his work is debated, and he reached about a century into the past.

options.label: The Archaic period
The Hellenistic period
The Greek Dark Ages
The Classical period

items.explain: The Classical period runs from the Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BC until Alexander's death in 323 BC.

items.prompt: Greece lost its power, yet its ideas reached much of Europe. What carried them there?

options.label: Greek city-states kept ruling those lands for centuries
Rome adopted Greek culture, especially philosophy, and spread variants of it

items.explain: Classical Greek culture, especially philosophy, influenced Rome, which propagated variants of it through the Mediterranean and much of Europe.

items.prompt: A Macedonian king marches east, and later Greek-style culture appears in Western Asia and Northern Africa. What explains this?

options.label: His conquests spread Greek culture, starting the Hellenistic period
Persian traders brought Greek customs home with them
Greek colonies settled there before the Archaic period
Rome moved Greek culture there before it had any influence

items.explain: Alexander's conquests spread Greek culture into Northern Africa and Western Asia, which is the Hellenistic period.

pack.title: Why Greece Stayed Divided
pack.question: Why was Greece a patchwork of city-states instead of one country?

beats.title: Why Greece Stayed Divided
beats.hook: For nearly all of its ancient history, Greece was not one country, and its landscape and history help explain why.

beats.prompt: The Mycenaean powers have collapsed, and Greek settlements sit in valleys separated by mountains. What kind of political units will grow up?
beats.explain: With no powerful states and many settlements separated by mountains, small independent city-states developed.

choices.label: Cities all answering to a foreign empire
choices.feedback: Outside rule is tempting, but the lack of any powerful state pushed the cities toward independence.

choices.label: One kingdom ruling the whole region
choices.feedback: A single ruler sounds natural, but no powerful state remained after the collapse and mountains kept settlements apart.

beats.prompt: Put these stages of Greek history in order.
beats.explain: The Dark Ages came first, then the Archaic period, then the Classical period, and the Hellenistic period followed.

paragraphs.heading: A world of city-states
paragraphs.text: Ancient Greece was a civilization made of many city-states and regions that shared related cultures and languages, grouped mainly around the northeastern Mediterranean Sea. It ran from the Greek Dark Ages, between the 12th and 9th centuries BC, until classical antiquity ended around 600 AD. Scholars trace its start back to Mycenaean Greece, which declined in the Bronze Age collapse around 1100 BC. Before Roman times, most of this area was officially unified just once, under the Kingdom of Macedon from 338 to 323 BC.

paragraphs.heading: Why the cities stayed small
paragraphs.text: The key political unit was the polis, or city-state. These began forming in the 8th century BC, opening the Archaic period, which lasted from about 800 to 500 BC. Once Mycenaean power fell, no strong states were left, and mountains cut many settlements off from their neighbours; together these pushed Greeks toward small, independent cities. In the same years Greeks founded colonies around the Mediterranean, reaching Al-Mina to the east by 800 BC and Ischia to the west by 775.

paragraphs.heading: Athens and Sparta take shape
paragraphs.text: Athens built its democracy step by step during the Archaic period. By the 7th century, every male citizen seems to have had the right to attend the assembly. Draco drew up a code of laws in 621 BC, and when tension between rich and poor went on, Solon was given power in 594 to make reforms that tried to balance the two. By the end of the 6th century the tyrant Hippias had been overthrown, and Cleisthenes made the system more democratic still. Sparta, meanwhile, developed rule by two kings, a council of elders and five ephors, and conquered neighbouring Messenia, turning its people into serfs.

paragraphs.heading: The Classical age
paragraphs.text: The Classical period ran from the Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BC to the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BC. Its style was later held up as the model of excellence, most famously in the Parthenon of Athens. Athens and its Delian League led in the 5th century, Sparta took over in the early 4th, and then power passed to Thebes and finally to the League of Corinth headed by Macedon. Three struggles shaped the age: the wars with Persia, the Peloponnesian War, and the rise of Macedon.

paragraphs.heading: Victory at Marathon
paragraphs.text: The wars with Persia began with a revolt. In 499 BC the Ionian city-states that Persia ruled rose against the tyrants Persia backed, and with troops from Athens and Eretria they reached and burned Sardis before being driven back; the revolt was crushed in 494. Darius I of Persia remembered that Athens had helped, and in 490 he gathered a fleet to punish it. At the Battle of Marathon the Athenians and their allies from Plataea, though badly outnumbered, beat the Persians, whose fleet then turned back.

paragraphs.heading: Greek culture spreads
paragraphs.text: Alexander's conquests carried Greek culture into North Africa and Western Asia. This Hellenistic period lasted from his death in 323 BC until Rome conquered the region. Rome itself was deeply shaped by Classical Greek culture, above all its philosophy, and passed versions of it on across the Mediterranean and much of Europe. That is why Classical Greece is usually called the cradle of Western civilization: the source of many basic ideas the modern West still draws on in politics, philosophy, science and art.

paragraphs.heading: How we know about it
paragraphs.text: Ancient Greece is the first period in world history recorded directly in full, connected histories rather than only in scraps such as king lists. Herodotus is often called the father of history, and later writers such as Thucydides, Xenophon and Plato followed him. Most of these writers were from Athens or on its side, so far more is known about Athens than about many other cities. They also wrote mostly about politics, war and diplomacy, and left economic and social life aside.
